summary: A pocket-sized OpenWrt box with three dedicated 2.4 GHz radios and a web interface built around PineAP, Hak5's rogue access point suite. It exists to impersonate access points that client devices are already looking for, capture handshakes, and run captive-portal attacks. The Basic model is 2.4 GHz only.
honest_take: The classic Pineapple attack chain has been substantially blunted since this hardware launched. WPA3 and 802.11w Protected Management Frames make forged deauthentication frames ineffective, iOS/Android/Windows all randomise MAC addresses and have largely stopped broadcasting directed probe requests for saved networks (which is what PineAP's karma attack feeds on), and HSTS plus universal HTTPS means a captive portal mostly gets you a browser warning rather than credentials. Hak5's own Enterprise documentation admits MFP 'prevents forged deauthentication packets from being respected by the client'. It is still a genuinely good and fast platform for auditing legacy WPA2 estates and open guest networks, but you are paying $250 for a single-core MIPS SoC and three cheap 2.4 GHz radios; the value is the software and the workflow, not the silicon.

price_note: Four tiers, and the spread is almost entirely licensing and services, not hardware. BASIC $850 = hardware, standard warranty, software update subscription, community support. STANDARD $1200 = same hardware plus a Cloud C2 Professional licence, extended warranty and standard support. ADVANCED (TAA) $2699.99 = TAA-compliant hardware with final assembly in the USA for MIL/GOV buyers, plus a Cloud C2 Teams Silver licence. PENTEST $6600 = the same $850 box plus a four-business-day wireless penetration test delivered by one Cobalt.io consultant over two weeks. A 1U rack mount is $160 extra. B2B SKU lists at $900.

summary: A 1U mains-powered rack unit with five dual-band radios and eight antennas, running the same PineAP software as the Mark VII but sized for permanent or long-running installation at a client site. The selling point is Plug-and-Provision: you ship it to the client, they plug it in, and you drive the whole thing remotely through a self-hosted Cloud C2 server.
honest_take: The hardware is real and considerably better than the Mark VII (Qualcomm IPQ4019 quad-core with two integrated radios, plus three MT7612U, 1 GB RAM, dual gigabit), but understand what the price ladder is selling. The $6600 'Pentest' tier is $850 of hardware plus a Cobalt.io consulting engagement; you are buying four consultant-days, not a better Pineapple. The $2699.99 Advanced tier's premium is TAA compliance for government procurement plus a Cloud C2 Teams licence. And the same 2026 reality check applies to all of them: Hak5's own Enterprise docs concede that Management Frame Protection 'prevents forged deauthentication packets from being respected by the client', so against a modern WPA3 or PMF-enabled estate the headline PineAP attacks largely do not land. What you are really getting is a very capable, remotely-managed, multi-radio 802.11 sensing and reporting platform.

name: WiFi Pineapple Pager
firmware_note: OpenWrt with a touch-free on-device UI, bash payloads extended with DuckyScript commands; Hak5 publishes the kernel patches and device tree.
price_note: $300 in black or yellow, in stock. Replacement battery $60, replacement clip $100. Glytch add-on mods sold separately: GPS $60, Mesh $60, Ethernet $40.
skill_note: The on-device menu makes recon approachable, but writing useful alert payloads means writing bash.
build_note: Charge, connect over USB-C, flash the current firmware through the browser; first flash takes 10-15 minutes.
summary: A belt-clip, battery-powered Pineapple with a colour screen, a d-pad, a buzzer and a vibration motor. It monitors 2.4, 5 and 6 GHz, runs PineAP, fires 'alert' payloads when it sees things like a deauth flood, and logs Wigle-compatible wardrives if you add a USB GPS. It is the first Pineapple you can genuinely walk around with.
honest_take: Hak5's marketing line that it is 'hundreds of times faster than other Pineapples' is about the radio, not the computer. The host SoC is the same MediaTek MT7628AN MIPS chip as the seven-year-old Mark VII - that is confirmed by Hak5's own published device tree file. The speed comes from a MediaTek MT7921U USB radio bolted alongside it, which is what supplies Wi-Fi 6/6E and Bluetooth. Battery life is about four hours, GPS is not included (it is a USB dongle you supply), and less than 32 MB of the internal flash overlay is free after firmware, so heavy package installs have to go to the 4 GB storage partition. Credit where due: the docs are unusually honest, stating outright that WPA3 and 802.11w PMF prevent injected disconnection packets and that injection is impossible on DFS and 6 GHz channels - 6 GHz mandates WPA3 even for 'open' networks. Buy it for tri-band recon and wardriving, not because you expect deauth to work.

name: WiFi Coconut
firmware_note: GPL userspace port of the Linux rt2800 kernel driver, so all 14 radios can be driven as one capture device on Linux, macOS and Windows.
price_note: Last listed at $200. Sold out, Hak5 says production is 'temporarily suspended' due to manufacturing shortages, and the product no longer appears in the shop's product navigation. Treat it as end-of-life; existing units are still supported.
skill_note: You need to already know why simultaneous multi-channel capture matters and be comfortable in Wireshark or Kismet.
build_note: Plug in over USB-C, install the open-source capture tools (Zadig driver replacement required on Windows).
summary: A USB-C device containing fourteen separate 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi radios, one per channel, so it can record the entire 2.4 GHz band simultaneously instead of channel-hopping and missing traffic. Output is standard pcap with radiotap headers, and it plugs straight into Kismet and Wireshark.
honest_take: It does exactly what it says and the engineering is genuinely clever - but be clear about what is inside. The radios enumerate as USB ID 148F:5370, which is the Ralink/MediaTek RT5370: a single-stream 802.11n 2.4 GHz chip that Hak5 themselves used to sell individually for $14.99. The Coconut is fourteen of those on a hub board. It is receive-only by design and Hak5 warns that transmitting may damage it and voids the warranty, so there is no injection, no deauth, no evil twin. It is 2.4 GHz only - no 5 GHz, no 6 GHz - which in 2026 means it misses most of the interesting traffic. It draws enough power that a Raspberry Pi 3 cannot run it. And the software repo has not been touched since February 2024 while the product itself has quietly left the shop navigation. Buy one secondhand only if wide-band 2.4 GHz capture is specifically your problem.

firmware_note: Adds a full web UI, three payload slots, a JAIL network mode and a DYNAMICPROXY stream interceptor over the original's switch-and-SSH workflow.

summary: A matchbox-sized OpenWrt computer with two Ethernet ports that you install between a target device and the wall jack. Traffic passes through it while it captures pcaps, spoofs DNS, tunnels out over VPN, or holds the target in a jail. It is powered over USB-C and managed from a web interface or remotely through Cloud C2.
honest_take: Understand the difference between this and a Plunder Bug before you buy either: the Packet Squirrel is INLINE and ACTIVE. It is a router in the path. It can modify, block, spoof and inject traffic, and it can route the target's traffic through your VPN. That power is also the risk - if it dies or you fumble a payload, you drop the target's network connection and you get noticed. honest_take: The single most important thing about this device is the thing beginners get wrong: out of the box it is NOT a passive tap. Hak5's own documentation says the USB-C tap port 'will also act as an additional Ethernet port on the target LAN' - it transmits by default, which means it can be seen, can respond to ARP, and puts you on the network. Passive 'mute' mode is a deliberate opt-in you enable by running plunderbug.ps1 or plunderbug.sh --mute on your laptop, and that setting lives on your host, not on the device. If you genuinely must not transmit - forensics, air-gapped environments, or anywhere that would notice a new MAC - use a real passive tap: Great Scott Gadgets' Throwing Star LAN Tap is an open-source PCB with no active components that costs about $15 to $40 and physically cannot transmit. name: USB Rubber Ducky
firmware_note: The 2022 hardware runs a compiled DuckyScript 3.0 payload (inject.bin) built in Hak5's browser-based PayloadStudio; DuckyScript 1.0 payloads still run unmodified.
price_note: $100 for the device, $110 Pro Bundle, $130 Elite Bundle - the bundles add PayloadStudio Pro and course access, not different hardware. B2B SKU $100. Replacement microSD card $20; spare coloured cases $20.
skill_note: Writing a first payload takes ten minutes. Writing one that survives a real target's timing, locale and EDR takes much longer.

summary: The device that invented keystroke injection as an attack class. It looks like a flash drive but enumerates as a keyboard, then types a pre-written payload at machine speed. The 2022 hardware added DuckyScript 3.0, a real structured language with variables, conditionals, loops and functions, plus out-of-band exfiltration.
honest_take: DuckyScript 3 is a genuine advance and not just marketing - you get IF/ELSE, WHILE, functions, integer variables, arithmetic and bitwise operators, VID/PID/manufacturer/serial spoofing, and Keystroke Reflection, which exfiltrates binary data back out through the keyboard's lock-key LED channel to loot.bin on the card. Nothing cheap does that last one. But be honest about the price: for pure 'type this script when plugged in', a $5 Digispark ATtiny85 or a $10-15 CH552 board does the job, and there are open-source projects that will run Ducky payloads on them. What you lose going cheap is real: no conditionals or host feedback, no reliable OS detection via lock-key state, no exfiltration channel, no VID/PID spoofing, ATtiny85 boards famously have flaky USB timing and enumerate slowly, and payload space is tiny, and Digispark boards use a fixed, well-known VID/PID that is trivial to blocklist. Two footnotes: Hak5 never publishes the microcontroller, though its own DFU recovery instructions give it away as an AT32UC3B1512; and the shop has carried backorder notices with multi-month batch queues.

name: Bash Bunny Mark II
firmware_note: Debian userland with an ATTACKMODE system that reconfigures the USB gadget personality on the fly; payloads are bash extended with QUACK-prefixed DuckyScript.
price_note: $200 for the Bash Bunny Mark II. A 'HotPlug Attack Combo Kit' bundling it with the USB Rubber Ducky and Shark Jack lists at $500.
skill_note: Bash plus an understanding of USB device classes, target OS behaviour, and what a machine will trust from a freshly-enumerated Ethernet adapter.
build_note: Flick the switch to arming mode, drop payloads on the mass-storage partition, flick to a payload slot.
summary: A small Linux computer in an oversized USB stick that impersonates several trusted USB devices at once - keyboard, gigabit Ethernet adapter, serial port and flash drive - to attack a machine from multiple angles simultaneously. The Mark II adds Bluetooth LE for geofencing and remote triggering, plus a microSD slot for mass exfiltration.
honest_take: The Bash Bunny's real weapon is not keystroke injection, it is USB Ethernet: when it enumerates as a network adapter, many operating systems will happily make it the default gateway and start sending traffic and credential material at it, which is what makes responder-style attacks so effective from a USB port. That is a genuinely different and more powerful class of attack than a Rubber Ducky. Two clarifications people get wrong. First, it does NOT run DuckyScript 3 - payloads are bash with QUACK-prefixed DuckyScript 1.0-derived commands, and Hak5's own docs tell you to append QUACK to most lines when porting a Ducky payload. Second, it has no Wi-Fi at all - a lot of secondary coverage gets this wrong. The only radio is Bluetooth LE, used for geofencing and remote triggers rather than as an attack radio, and the Bunny reaches a network only by tethering off the host it is plugged into. It is also not a Cloud C2 device. Worth noting that Hak5's own comparison table shows identical CPU and storage for the Mark I and Mark II while the prose alongside it claims faster performance and doubled RAM; the real, verifiable deltas are the microSD slot and BLE. At $200 for five-year-old silicon whose part number Hak5 has never published, this is priced on capability, not components.

summary: A charging cable with an implant built into the connector housing. It works as a real cable, but it also runs a web server on its own Wi-Fi, stores DuckyScript payloads, injects keystrokes into whatever it is plugged into, and on Elite models logs keystrokes from a keyboard plugged through it. It is visually indistinguishable from a normal cable.
honest_take: The implant's brain is an ESP8266 - the shipped firmware binary literally contains the string 'Firmware ONLY supports ESP8266!!!'. Not an ESP32 and not a custom ASIC; a CT scan found two dies in one package, which is custom packaging, not custom silicon. There is no separate USB chip either: the ESP8266 has no USB peripheral, so USB is bit-banged in software using the open-source cnlohr/espusb stack. That sets a hard ceiling - 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi only, no Bluetooth, low-speed USB, and storage measured in kilobytes. What $150-220 buys is the engineering that fits all that inside a connector housing that still looks and works like a cable, which genuinely nobody else does as well. Three things to weigh. The tier matters far more than the connector: Basic is 8 payload slots, ~4,000 keystrokes and 120 keys/sec with no keylogger; Elite is 50-300 slots, ~1.5 million keystrokes, 890 keys/sec, the keylogger and the C2. The 'geo-fencing' feature is not GPS - it is Wi-Fi SSID presence detection, so it fences on 'is this network in range', not on location. And the firmware is closed with a EULA that forbids reverse engineering, so you cannot audit the cable you are about to plug into a client's machine.

hardware.mcu_primary_note: Confirmed three ways: the shipped firmware binary contains the literal string 'Firmware ONLY supports ESP8266!!!' along with Espressif NONOS SDK markers; Mischief Gadgets' flash.py instantiates ESP8266ROM; and the flash layout uses the ESP8266 signature offsets. The published memory map ships exactly two profiles, 1024 KB and 2048 KB, which is the Basic and Elite split. Independent teardown work found the Wi-Fi OUI DC:4F:22, which is Espressif.
hardware.mcu_secondary_note: There is NO separate USB controller. The ESP8266 has no USB peripheral at all, so USB is bit-banged in software on GPIO using the open-source cnlohr/espusb stack - Mike Grover credited cnlohr for that work in 2019. This is why the device is limited to low-speed USB and why 'USB overclock' is even a meaningful setting (120 keys/sec on Basic, 890 on Elite): you can only overclock a software stack. A Lumafield industrial CT scan found a second silicon die bonded under the main processor, so the 'custom silicon' framing refers to custom packaging of two dies, not a custom ASIC.
